subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 44-year-old man who works as a wildlife rehabilitator in Texas presents with several years of progressive painless burns and ulcers on his hands and feet, which he cannot feel when he touches hot objects. Examination shows diffuse thickening of the skin of the face with prominent earlobes and eyebrows, and multiple nodular lesions over the trunk and extremities. Skin biopsy shows numerous acid-fast bacilli.
question: Which of the following best explains the distribution of this patient's lesions?

options.text: The organism replicates in sweat glands, producing local skin destruction only
The organism prefers cooler temperatures, so it infects skin and superficial nerves of the extremities and face
The organism spreads hematogenously to the central nervous system, causing sensory loss centrally
Bacterial toxins destroy motor neurons with a length-dependent pattern
Immune complexes deposit in the small vessels of acral skin, causing ischemic neuropathy

explanation_correct: Mycobacterium leprae is an acid-fast bacillus that prefers cool temperatures, so it infects skin and superficial nerves, producing the classic glove-and-stocking loss of sensation that leads to unrecognized trauma, burns, and ulcers. This patient's diffuse facial infiltration with thickened skin and nodular lesions is the leonine facies of the lepromatous form. The armadillo is a noted reservoir in the United States.

explanation_incorrect.A: The distribution reflects temperature preference broadly across skin and nerves, not selective tropism for sweat glands.
explanation_incorrect.C: Leprosy does not cause central nervous system disease; the sensory loss results from infection of cool superficial peripheral nerves.
explanation_incorrect.D: The neuropathy is sensory and results from direct nerve infection, not from a toxin that kills motor neurons.
explanation_incorrect.E: Immune-complex vasculitis is not the mechanism; the lesions reflect direct bacillary infiltration of skin and nerves.

educationalObjective: M leprae prefers cool temperatures, causing infection of skin and superficial nerves with glove-and-stocking sensory loss.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 36-year-old man from a region with endemic leprosy has a small number of well-demarcated, hypopigmented, hairless plaques on the trunk. Sensation within the plaques is diminished. Skin biopsy shows few organisms and a predominantly Th1-pattern lymphocytic infiltrate with granulomas. He is diagnosed with the tuberculoid form of leprosy.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the immunologic basis of the tuberculoid form of leprosy compared with the lepromatous form?

options.text: High cell-mediated immunity with a largely Th1 response and a low bacterial load
Low cell-mediated immunity with a largely Th2 response and a high bacterial load
Absent antibody production with immune-complex mediated nerve destruction
Neutrophil-predominant inflammation with abscess formation in peripheral nerves
Autoantibodies against myelin basic protein causing demyelinating neuropathy

explanation_correct: The tuberculoid form is characterized by high cell-mediated immunity with a largely Th1 response and a low bacterial load, which limits disease to a few hypoesthetic, hairless skin plaques. The lepromatous form is the opposite: low cell-mediated immunity, a largely Th2 response, high bacterial burden, diffuse skin involvement, and leonine facies. Many cases fall between the two extremes.

explanation_incorrect.B: This describes exactly the lepromatous pole, which is diffuse, communicable, and potentially lethal because of the high bacterial load.
explanation_incorrect.C: Antibody production is not absent in tuberculoid leprosy; the protective arm here is cell-mediated immunity, and nerve injury is from bacilli and inflammation rather than immune complexes.
explanation_incorrect.D: Leprosy lesions are granulomatous with lymphocytes and macrophages, not neutrophil-rich abscesses.
explanation_incorrect.E: This describes an autoimmune demyelinating process such as Guillain-Barre, not leprosy, in which nerve damage follows direct bacillary involvement.

educationalObjective: Tuberculoid leprosy reflects a strong Th1 cell-mediated response with few organisms and limited hypoesthetic plaques, whereas lepromatous leprosy reflects a Th2-predominant response with a high bacillary load.

subject: Microbiology
vignette: A 52-year-old man with lepromatous leprosy and extensive nodular skin lesions is started on therapy chosen for his high bacterial burden. His brother, who has only a few hypoesthetic plaques and is diagnosed with tuberculoid leprosy, is started on a simpler regimen.
question: Which of the following best explains why clofazimine is added to this patient's regimen?

options.text: Clofazimine replaces dapsone when dapsone resistance develops in the tuberculoid form
Clofazimine provides rapid relief of nerve pain in tuberculoid disease
Clofazimine is a vaccine adjuvant given with BCG in lepromatous disease
The lepromatous form has a high bacterial burden and is treated with rifampin and dapsone plus clofazimine
Clofazimine is needed to treat coexisting tuberculosis

explanation_correct: Tuberculoid leprosy is treated with dapsone and rifampin, whereas clofazimine is added for the lepromatous form, which carries a much higher bacterial load and is communicable. The mnemonic given is that dapsone and rifampin cover the tuberculoid form while the lepromatous form needs the additional agent. Clofazimine is not an antituberculous drug.

explanation_incorrect.A: The added agent is for the lepromatous form's higher burden; tuberculoid disease is treated with dapsone and rifampin alone.
explanation_incorrect.B: Clofazimine is not an analgesic and does not treat nerve pain; neuropathic pain in leprosy is managed separately.
explanation_incorrect.C: BCG is a vaccine given before exposure and is not combined with clofazimine as an adjuvant in treatment.
explanation_incorrect.E: Clofazimine is an antileprosy agent; coexisting tuberculosis would require standard antituberculous drugs such as isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.

educationalObjective: Tuberculoid leprosy is treated with dapsone and rifampin, while clofazimine is added for the lepromatous form because of its high bacterial load.
